steps.text: Write the introduction for a graph learning paper that extends graph attention networks to heterophilic graphs using directional, non-local neighborhood information. Cover the background on GNNs and GAT, the heterophily problem, our contributions, and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) combine graph signal processing and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and they have got remarkable results on machine learning tasks with non-Euclidean data. In CNNs the neighbours get different weights, but in the vanilla GNNs and in many other popular variants the convolutional kernel gives the same weight to every node in a neighbourhood. The Graph Attention Network (GAT) fixes this limitation by letting nodes connect to their local neighbours with learnable weights.

GAT builds the node representation only from the representations of its direct neighbours. This works well on homophilic graphs, where a node and its neighbours probably have the same label. But on heterophilic graphs, where nodes from different classes tend to be connected, GAT loses a lot of performance in node classification tasks.

- Contributions
  - non-local neighborhood info helps with heterophily; not yet in GAT
  - (1) parameterized normalized graph Laplacians; directional aggregation; normalized Laplacians as special cases; adjust diffusion/spectral distances
  - (2) theorem: spectral distance as surrogate for diffusion distance; cheaper; extends earlier work
  - (3) DGAT: topology-guided rewiring; global directional attention
  - beats SOTA across homophily levels; integrates with GAT and other attention mechanisms
- Organization: Sec 2 background; Sec 3 Laplacian, theory, DGAT; Sec 4 related work; Sec 5 experiments

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) combine graph signal processing and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and they have got remarkable results on machine learning tasks with non-Euclidean data. In CNNs the neighbours get different weights, but in the vanilla GNNs and in many other popular variants the convolutional kernel gives the same weight to every node in a neighbourhood. The Graph Attention Network (GAT) fixes this limitation by letting nodes connect to their local neighbours with learnable weights.

GAT builds the node representation only from the representations of its direct neighbours. This works well on homophilic graphs, where a node and its neighbours probably have the same label. But on heterophilic graphs, where nodes from different classes tend to be connected, GAT loses a lot of performance in node classification tasks.

Non-local neighborhood information has been found to help GNNs with the heterophily problem, but it has not been used in the GAT model, and this is what we address in this paper. Our main contributions are: (1) We propose a new class of parameterized normalized graph Laplacian matrices that give better control over directional aggregation, and the widely used normalized Laplacians are special cases of it. With the parameters of the new Laplacian we can change the spectral property of the graph, and this adjusts the diffusion distances and spectral distances between nodes; (2) We prove a theorem that lets us use the spectral distance as a surrogate function for the diffusion distance, so comparing the relative distance between nodes costs much less computation. This extends the scope of earlier work by a lot and overcomes some of its shortcomings. (3) Using the new graph Laplacian, we propose the Directional Graph Attention Network (DGAT). DGAT contributes two things: i. a graph rewiring strategy guided by topology, with theoretical justifications; ii. a global directional attention that allows topological-aware information propagation. The experiments show that DGAT is effective and better than SOTA GNNs for node classification on graphs with different homophily levels. The strategy is flexible and can be integrated seamlessly with the original GAT architecture and with other kinds of graph attention mechanism.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section 2 introduces notation and background knowledge; Section 3 proposes the new class of Laplacian, shows its properties, proves the theoretical results on spectral and diffusion distances and presents the DGAT architecture; Section 4 discusses related works; Section 5 shows the experimental results and comparisons on synthetic and real-world graphs.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Combining graph signal processing and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [1], Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable results on machine learning tasks with non-Euclidean data [2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10]. Unlike CNNs, where neighbours are weighted differently, the convolutional kernel in the vanilla GNNs [3] and many other popular variants [4,6] assigns the same weight within a neighbourhood. The Graph Attention Network (GAT) [5] overcomes this limitation by allowing nodes to connect to their local neighbours with learnable weights.

The GAT model generates a node's representation solely from the representations of its direct neighbours, which works well on homophilic graphs [11], where a node and its neighbours are likely to share the same label. However, GAT suffers significant performance loss in node classification tasks on heterophilic graphs [12,13], where nodes from different classes tend to be connected.

Non-local neighborhood information has been found helpful for dealing with the heterophily problem in GNNs [14,15,12,16,17], but it has not been leveraged in the GAT model; we address this issue in this paper. The main contributions of our paper are: (1) We propose a new class of parameterized normalized graph Laplacian matrices, which give better control over directional aggregation and contain the widely used normalized Laplacians as special cases. Through the parameters of the new Laplacian, we can adjust the diffusion distances and spectral distances between nodes by altering the spectral property of the graph; (2) We establish a theorem that enables using the spectral distance as a surrogate function of the diffusion distance, which significantly reduces the computational cost of comparing relative distances between nodes. This substantially extends the scope of [8] and overcomes some of its shortcomings. (3) Based on the new graph Laplacian, we propose the Directional Graph Attention Network (DGAT). The contributions of DGAT are twofold: i. a topology-guided graph rewiring strategy with theoretical justifications; ii. a global directional attention that enables topological-aware information propagation. The empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of DGAT over SOTA GNNs for node classification on graphs across various homophily levels. The proposed strategy is flexible and integrates seamlessly with the original GAT architecture and other types of graph attention mechanism.

The paper is organized as follows: notation and background knowledge are introduced in Section 2; in Section 3, we propose the new class of Laplacian, show its properties, prove the theoretical results on spectral and diffusion distances and present the DGAT architecture; in Section 4, we discuss related works; in Section 5, we show experimental results and comparisons on synthetic and real-world graphs.
